claims.text: The initial refractory high-entropy alloy is produced by conventional powder metallurgy.
The initial alloy has a homogeneous matrix.
The initial alloy lacks oxide dispersoids.
The proposed intervention is to introduce a 1–3 vol% fraction of nanoscale Y2O3 through mechanical alloying and consolidated sintering.
Optimized milling and sintering will produce a uniform nanometer-scale Y2O3 dispersion and avoid agglomeration.
The Y2O3 dispersoids will remain stable under high-temperature and irradiation conditions.
Y2O3 nanoparticles pin dislocation motion.
Dislocation pinning by Y2O3 produces dispersion strengthening.
Y2O3 nanoparticles act as sinks for irradiation-induced defects.
Y2O3 nanoparticles slow the migration of irradiation-induced defects.
Y2O3 nanoparticles slow the recombination of irradiation-induced defects.
Y2O3 dispersoids inhibit grain-boundary mobility.
The dispersoids reduce radiation-induced embrittlement.
The modified alloy will have greater yield strength than the unmodified alloy.
The modified alloy will have greater creep resistance than the unmodified alloy.
The strength and creep improvements will occur without loss of ductility.
The modified alloy will exhibit delayed grain growth.
The modified alloy will exhibit less irradiation-induced damage than the unmodified alloy.
The predicted benefits are expected at approximately 1000°C or above and around a neutron fluence of 10^21 n/m².
Nonuniform or agglomerated Y2O3 may compromise the improvements and create localized weaknesses.

contradictions.description: The boundary conditions state that benefits are expected only when dispersion is uniform, but the falsification rule treats nonuniform dispersion and its resulting degradation as falsification. That outcome could instead indicate failure to implement the stipulated intervention.

The mechanism says the particles slow defect recombination while also attributing reduced irradiation damage to their defect-sink behavior. Slower recombination does not coherently explain removal of irradiation-induced defects or reduced retained damage without an additional mechanism.
